tip: ‘Silakan’ invites someone to do something for their own benefit: ‘silakan duduk’ = please have a seat. ‘Tolong’ is the other 'please' – it asks someone to help you.
Commands are negated with ‘jangan’, not ‘tidak’: ‘jangan pergi’ = don't go. ‘Tidak’ only states facts (‘dia tidak pergi’ = he doesn't go) – it can't forbid anything.
‘Nanti’ in a warning means 'or else': ‘nanti sakit perut’ = you'll get a stomachache.
‘Boleh saya pinjam’ asks permission (may I borrow). ‘Bisa’ is ability (can): ‘saya bisa berenang’ = I can swim. English 'can' covers both jobs; Indonesian splits them.
‘Coba’ before a verb softens a suggestion: ‘coba tanya’ = try asking.
‘Mari kita’ + verb = 'let's': ‘mari kita mulai’ = let's begin. ‘Mari’ is the polite version – among friends you'll hear ‘ayo’ instead: ‘ayo mulai!’
‘Ber-’ turns a noun into 'do X': ‘berfoto’ = take a photo.
‘Kalau’ = if/when in everyday speech: ‘kalau ada masalah’ = if there is a problem.
Time words do the past-tense work: ‘kemarin saya pergi’ = yesterday I went. The verb never changes.
‘Tadi’ = earlier today: ‘tadi pagi’ = this morning (already past).
‘Waktu’ opens a past when-clause: ‘waktu saya kecil...’ = when I was little...
‘Lalu’ after a time word = last: ‘bulan lalu’ = last month, ‘minggu lalu’ = last week.
‘Terus’ strings actions in speech: ‘terus lupa’ = and then (I) forgot.
‘Tutup’ never changes for tense – ‘sudah’ alone tells you the shop 'was already closed': ‘sudah tutup’. Time in Indonesian lives in the markers, not in verb endings.
‘Lalu’ after a time span = ago: ‘dua hari lalu’ = two days ago.
‘Dulu’ after a verb means first, not long ago: ‘membeli tiket dulu’ = buy a ticket first. At the start of a sentence, ‘dulu’ means back in the day.
Duration 'for' is ‘selama’, not ‘untuk’: ‘mati selama dua jam’ = out for two hours. ‘Untuk’ is 'for' as purpose or recipient (‘untuk kamu’ = for you).
‘Sakit’ + body part = it hurts: ‘sakit kepala’ = headache, ‘sakit perut’ = stomachache.
English needs 'has had a fever since' – Indonesian states it flat: ‘demam sejak kemarin malam’, no tense change. ‘Sejak’ alone signals it started then and still holds.
You drink medicine in Indonesian, even pills: ‘minum obat’ is literally 'drink medicine'. There's no separate 'take' verb for it.
‘Capek’ is the everyday spoken 'tired': ‘badan saya capek’. The formal counterpart is ‘lelah’ – same meaning, but ‘capek’ is what you'll actually hear in conversation.
‘Bilang’ is the conversational 'say': ‘dokter bilang’ = the doctor said. Formal writing prefers ‘berkata’ or ‘mengatakan’ – ‘bilang’ is for speech.
‘Ke-...-an’ builds nouns: ‘sehat’ (healthy) becomes ‘kesehatan’ (health).
‘Terus’ after a verb = keeps on: ‘batuk terus’ = keeps coughing.
‘-nya’ on a noun here means his or her: ‘giginya’ = his tooth (‘gigi’ + ‘-nya’). No separate word for 'his' – the owner hangs off the end of the noun.
‘Rumah sakit’, literally 'sick house', is the word for hospital. Indonesian compounds put the main noun first – ‘rumah’ (house) is the thing, ‘sakit’ just describes it.
‘Di-’ flips the verb passive: ‘diminum’ = is taken (drunk).
The ‘-nya’ on ‘cuacanya’ isn't 'its' here – it marks the weather as the known topic, like English 'the': ‘cuacanya cerah’ = the weather is clear.
‘Kalau’ starts an if-clause; no 'then' word needed after the comma: ‘kalau hujan, saya naik taksi’.
Indonesian skips the 'it' in 'it's raining' – ‘hujan’ is a verb on its own. ‘Sedang’ marks in progress: ‘sedang hujan deras’ = raining hard right now.
